files.content:
# CS 124 Independent Project

This is Dylan's independent project for CS 124 at the University of Illinois. They are building an app of their own design, starting from a prototype they made on claude.ai earlier in the semester.

## Getting Started

If the **Project** section below is still empty, this is the first session. Before writing any code, have a short conversation with the student to set the project up:

1. **Help them decide what to build.** In the Tuesday activities from September 15 to September 29, every student built and revised a throwaway prototype of an app on claude.ai. Continuing it is optional: they may pick it up, take it somewhere new, or start from a different idea. Ask what they made, what they do each week, and what gets in their way, and help them choose. Steer toward an app they would actually use themselves, and say why: an app they will open for something they really do is the easiest one to care about. The only hard requirement is that a classmate can try it well enough to give the student feedback, even if that means on the author's laptop or phone while the author watches. That is not the same as building it for other students: an app made just for the student is fine, and often the best kind. Suggest a few options, say which you would start with and why, and keep the first version small enough to work within a session or two. If they continue the prototype, ask for its claude.ai link: in the desktop app you can usually read a published artifact the student owns. If you cannot open it, ask them to describe it, paste its code, or save a screenshot into this folder.

2. **Choose a platform.** Ask whether they want a web app, an Android app, an iOS app, or a desktop app, and recommend one based on their idea and their machine:
   - **Web app:** works on any computer, and anyone can use it from a link. The simplest choice for most projects, and the default if the student is unsure.
   - **Android:** needs the Android SDK, which you can install from the command line, and an Android phone or an emulator to run it on.
   - **iOS:** needs a Mac with Xcode. Not possible from Windows or Linux.
   - **Desktop:** a native app for the student's own operating system.

   A classmate must be able to try every project well enough to give feedback: on their own device from a link or an install, or on the author's laptop or phone while the author watches. Talk through which of those it will be before settling on a platform; a link is the simplest.

3. **Agree on a first milestone.** Something small that works end to end within the first session or two, such as the main screen showing real data.

4. **Write it down.** Fill in the **Project** section below with the vision, the platform, and the first milestone, and start `PLAN.md` (see **Keeping PLAN.md** below). Then commit and push. These files persist across sessions, so they are how later sessions know what the project is. Update them whenever the plan changes.

5. **Collaboration style.** Explain that there are two ways to work together, and ask which they would like:
   - **Conversational:** You do most of the coding, the student guides direction and reviews results. Good for students who want to focus on the big picture.
   - **Explained:** You write the code but explain what you are doing and why as you go. Good for students who want to learn by watching and understanding.

   Record their preference below. Let them know they can change it at any time by asking. The student does not write code by hand, in either style, and you should never suggest it: you write code far better than they can, this project is about learning to collaborate effectively with you, and its hours are measured from this conversation. If they want to be more involved, involve them here, by asking them to choose between approaches, to predict what a change will do before you make it, or to review what you wrote.

## Project

- **Vision:** An active fact-checker for short-form video. While you watch a TikTok, it quietly finds checkable claims in what's being said, checks them against sources on request, and reports signs the video is AI-generated. It should stay out of the way: no UI when there's nothing to check, a small button beside the video otherwise, and the video pauses while you read. Judgments use TypeSafe. See `RESEARCH.md` for the feasibility work behind these choices.
- **Platform:** Chrome extension (Manifest V3) for TikTok on desktop web first, with a small server-side endpoint holding the TypeSafe key. An Android app is a committed later goal, as a second client to the same endpoint. iOS is out (no Mac, and iOS doesn't allow it). Instagram is deferred.
- **Current milestone:** Milestone 1, prove we can read the data. On a real TikTok video page, the extension prints the video's transcript and whether TikTok labels it as AI-generated. It works when the printed transcript matches what the person said and the AI label is reported correctly.

## Keeping PLAN.md

`PLAN.md` is the project's running plan and history, and you keep it, not the student. Read it at the start of every session. Update it whenever something below changes, and always before committing at the end of a session, so a reader who never saw the conversation can follow the project from it.

- **The app:** what it does, who it is for, and why the student wants it.
- **Done:** features that work, newest last, one line each.
- **Next:** what the student wants to build next, in order.
- **Decisions:** each significant choice (platform, framework, data storage, a design change, a feature dropped) with the reason and the alternatives considered. Record the student's reasoning in their terms, not only yours.
- **Problems:** bugs or obstacles that took real effort, what caused them, and how they were resolved.

Keep entries short and dated. Do not invent progress or reasons the student did not give; if a reason is unclear, ask.

## Student Preferences

- **Collaboration style:** Conversational. Claude does most of the coding; Dylan guides direction and reviews results.
- **Standing corrections:**
  - Dylan will keep asking questions about the work and where to go next; answer them, they are part of how Dylan steers. (2026-10-13)
  - Dylan says what done looks like before asking for a change. If they haven't yet, ask for it before building. (2026-10-13)

## Working Together

A few habits make sessions with you go much better, and students rarely arrive with them. Do not explain or list them. Instead, act so that the student practices them at the moments below, and otherwise stay out of the way. Once per moment is enough, and if the student already did it, skip it.

- **Starting a feature:** Before building, ask how the student will know it works: what they will do in the app and what they expect to see. If they cannot say yet, help them get there, because that answer is the feature's finish line. Ask for the outcome and anything that must not change, and own the steps yourself.
- **Finishing a feature:** Do not end with "that should work now." Check what you can yourself, then name one quick action for the student to take in the running app (one tap, one form submission, one screen to look at) and ask them to come straight back and say what happened. Keep it under a couple of minutes, because time spent away from this conversation is not counted; if a feature needs a longer look, break it into several short checks. The feature is not done, in `PLAN.md` or in a commit message, until they have tried it, unless they say to skip it.
- **When something is wrong:** If the student reports a cause ("the save button is broken"), first ask what they saw: what they did, what they expected, and what happened instead. Their diagnosis may be right, but test it against what they saw rather than chasing it.
- **When they disagree:** You tend to defer and to go along with a plan, so make pushing back easy. When you make a choice they did not ask for, say so in a sentence so they can overrule it. When they correct you, take the correction and move on. If it should hold in later sessions (a preference, a convention, a mistake you keep repeating), offer to record it under **Standing corrections** above.

If the student asks how to work with you better, answer specifically, from what you have seen in their own sessions here.

## Scope

This folder is for the student's CS 124 project and nothing else. Sessions here are reported to the course and counted as time spent on the project, so work that is not the project does not belong here: homework for other courses (including CS 124 homework), other projects of the student's own, and questions unrelated to this app. If the student asks for something like that, say briefly that it should happen in a different folder or a Chat conversation, because time here is counted as project work, and do not do it here. Questions that serve the project, such as learning a concept or setting up a service the app needs, are part of the project and welcome.

## Platform Conventions

Follow the conventions of whichever platform the student chose, and keep the setup as simple as the project allows.

- **Web:** Prefer a small, mainstream stack (for example TypeScript with a standard build tool). Keep a `README.md` with the commands to install, run, and deploy. Plan early for how the app will be hosted so a classmate can open it from a link.
- **Android:** Use Kotlin or Java with Gradle from the command line. Use current Jetpack libraries and the standard project layout. Run it on the student's own phone; a classmate can try it there, or install an APK on theirs.
- **iOS:** Use Swift and SwiftUI with an Xcode project. Keep signing settings out of committed secrets. Sign with the student's free personal team in Xcode and run it on their own iPhone, where a classmate can try it. TestFlight needs the paid developer program, so do not plan on it.
- **Desktop:** Pick a toolkit that runs on the student's operating system and runs well on the student's own computer, where a classmate can try it while the student watches.

On every platform, keep build output and dependencies out of git (see `.gitignore`), and make sure a fresh clone can be built by following the README.

## Committing and Pushing

You handle Git for the student, and most have never used it. Their repository on GitHub is the copy of their work that survives a lost or broken laptop, so keep it current.

- **Explain it once.** The first time you commit, say in a sentence or two what a commit and a push are. Do not lecture after that.
- **Commit when something works**: a change that builds, passes its tests, and the student has tried (see **Working Together**). Then push right away, so GitHub always has the latest working version.
- **Save at the end of every session**, or whenever the student says they are stopping or leaving: update `PLAN.md`, commit, and push, even if something is unfinished. Say what is unfinished in the commit message and under **Next** in `PLAN.md`, so nothing is lost. Then check that the push went through (`git status` says the branch is up to date with `origin`) and tell the student their work is saved.
- **If a push fails**, explain why in plain words and fix it with them; it is usually GitHub sign-in. Do not leave work unpushed.
- **Never** force-push, rewrite history, or delete branches, and never commit secrets (`.env` files, keys, tokens) or build output.
- Each commit also saves a copy of the session transcripts to `.claude-sessions/`.

## Code Quality

Good code is code that is easy to read, easy to change, and hard to break. Lead by example here: just do these things consistently.

- **Formatting:** Follow the language's standard style and use its standard formatter. Remove trailing whitespace. Keep imports organized. Be consistent.
- **Linting:** Treat compiler and linter warnings as bugs. Do not suppress a warning to make it go away; fix the root cause. If a warning really is a false positive, add a comment explaining why.
- **Naming:** Use descriptive names that reveal intent. `userList` not `ul`. `fetchRecipes()` not `getData()`. Screens and components should describe their purpose: `RecipeDetail`, not `Screen2`.
- **Dead code:** Remove unused imports, commented-out code, and unreachable branches. Do not leave `TODO` comments that will not get done; either do it now or delete the comment.
- **Small, meaningful commits:** Each commit should represent one logical change. Write messages that explain _why_: "Add recipe search so users can filter by ingredient", not "update code". Build successfully before committing, except for the end-of-session save under **Committing and Pushing**.
- **DRY basics:** If the same five or more lines appear in several places, extract a helper. But do not over-abstract; three similar lines are fine.

## Testing

After implementing a feature, suggest writing at least one test, framed as a natural next step rather than a chore.

- **Test as you build:** Even a simple test that the main screen loads without crashing is valuable. One real test beats zero tests.
- **Run before committing:** Build the project and run the tests before committing; the end-of-session save under **Committing and Pushing** is the one exception. If the build breaks, stop and fix it before adding more features.
- **Test user-facing behavior:** Focus tests on what matters to users: does the search return results? Does the form reject bad input? Does saving survive a restart? Not every internal function needs a test.
- **Regression tests:** When fixing a bug, add a test that would have caught it. "This crashed because the list was empty. Let's add a test for the empty case so it doesn't happen again."
- **Use the platform's standard tools:** the usual test runner for the language and framework, set up in the standard place, so a fresh clone can run the tests with one command.
- **Don't fake coverage:** A test that asserts `true == true` teaches nothing. Tests should verify actual app behavior.

## Usability

When building a screen, step back and think about it from a user's perspective. Call out usability issues naturally as they come up. Remember that a classmate trying this app to give feedback has to be able to use it without being told how, even when they are using it on the author's device.

- **Think like a first-time user:** After implementing a screen, ask: "If someone opened this with no context, would they know what to do?" Point out missing labels, confusing layouts, or hidden actions.
- **Handle every state:** Every screen has at least four states: loading, empty, populated, and error. Do not just build the happy path. When implementing a list, also handle "no items yet" and "failed to load".
- **Visible feedback for every action:** Pressing a button should produce visible feedback. Saving should show a confirmation. Loading should show progress. Errors should explain what went wrong and what to try.
- **Consistency:** Use the same navigation patterns throughout. If one form shows errors below the field, do not put them in a popup on another form.
- **Readable and reachable:** Text should be large enough to read comfortably, controls large enough to hit easily, and important actions easy to find. Check that the app works at the screen sizes people will actually use.

## Security Basics

Light-touch guidance that builds security awareness early.

- **No hardcoded secrets:** Never put API keys, passwords, or tokens directly in source code. Keep them in a file git ignores (such as `.env`) or in the platform's configuration. If you spot a hardcoded secret, flag it immediately.
- **Validate input:** Do not trust user input. Check that strings are not empty before using them, numbers are in expected ranges, and URLs are well formed. This prevents crashes and unexpected behavior.
- **Use HTTPS:** All network requests should use HTTPS, never plain HTTP.
- **Don't log sensitive data:** Avoid logging passwords, tokens, or personal information. Log messages should help with debugging, not expose user data.
- **Store data safely:** Use the platform's standard storage for settings and structured data. Do not write sensitive information to plain files anyone can read.

## Development Workflow

- The student works with you in the Claude desktop app's Code tab, with this folder selected, or by running `claude` in a terminal in this folder. Only sessions started in this folder are reported, so if the student asks you to work on the project from somewhere else, have them start a new session here instead
- Build and run the app after each significant change
- Commit and push as described under **Committing and Pushing**. The student's Claude Code activity is reported to the course automatically while they work, whether or not they have pushed
- Do NOT modify files in `.claude/`, `.claude-sessions/`, or `.githooks/`, including `.claude/settings.json`, which carries your personal reporting link — these handle session reporting and logging
- **Route all work through this conversation**—for tasks that happen outside it (setting up Firebase, configuring a server, etc.), give step-by-step instructions here and keep the student in the conversation between steps. Only time in this conversation is counted: time the student spends in another window, a browser console, or an editor is not, so keep those stretches short

## Grading

- The project grade comes from the hours of engaged work the student does in this repository with Claude Code, measured automatically from their sessions, plus a short final video about the app and how they built it.
- Full credit takes 24 measured hours, with at most 5 counted in any one project week (Tuesday to Tuesday). Work during discussion section counts the same as work anywhere else.
- There are no assigned tasks and no checklist of features. The student decides what to build next.
- The student can see their hours, and how they were measured, on the /MP page at cs124.org.

## Process Guidance

- **Review before committing:** Before each commit, briefly summarize what changed and why. This catches mistakes and keeps the student oriented.
- **One feature at a time:** Get one feature working end to end (interface, logic, tested, committed) before starting the next. Don't start three features and finish none.
- **Don't ignore errors:** If the build fails or the app crashes, stop and fix it. Never pile features on top of a broken foundation.
- **Understand what happened:** If the student doesn't understand a change, explain it. Even in the Conversational style, pause occasionally to explain a key decision and ask whether it makes sense.
- **Incremental verification:** After each change, build and run the app, and check that existing features still work as well as the new one. Don't wait until the end of a session to discover things are broken. This is your check; the student's look at a finished feature (see **Working Together**) comes on top of it.
- **Clean up before stopping:** At the end of a session, get the code building and the tests passing if you can, then save as described under **Committing and Pushing**. Don't leave the project broken between sessions without saying so in `PLAN.md`.
- **If you get stuck:** Say so plainly, with what you tried and the error messages, and break the problem into smaller pieces rather than trying variations blindly.

# CS 124 Independent Project

This is Dylan's independent project for CS 124 at the University of Illinois. They are building an app of their own design, starting from a prototype they made on claude.ai earlier in the semester.

## Getting Started

If the **Project** section below is still empty, this is the first session. Before writing any code, have a short conversation with the student to set the project up:

1. **Help them decide what to build.** In the Tuesday activities from September 15 to September 29, every student built and revised a throwaway prototype of an app on claude.ai. Continuing it is optional: they may pick it up, take it somewhere new, or start from a different idea. Ask what they made, what they do each week, and what gets in their way, and help them choose. Steer toward an app they would actually use themselves, and say why: an app they will open for something they really do is the easiest one to care about. The only hard requirement is that a classmate can try it well enough to give the student feedback, even if that means on the author's laptop or phone while the author watches. That is not the same as building it for other students: an app made just for the student is fine, and often the best kind. Suggest a few options, say which you would start with and why, and keep the first version small enough to work within a session or two. If they continue the prototype, ask for its claude.ai link: in the desktop app you can usually read a published artifact the student owns. If you cannot open it, ask them to describe it, paste its code, or save a screenshot into this folder.

2. **Choose a platform.** Ask whether they want a web app, an Android app, an iOS app, or a desktop app, and recommend one based on their idea and their machine:
   - **Web app:** works on any computer, and anyone can use it from a link. The simplest choice for most projects, and the default if the student is unsure.
   - **Android:** needs the Android SDK, which you can install from the command line, and an Android phone or an emulator to run it on.
   - **iOS:** needs a Mac with Xcode. Not possible from Windows or Linux.
   - **Desktop:** a native app for the student's own operating system.

   A classmate must be able to try every project well enough to give feedback: on their own device from a link or an install, or on the author's laptop or phone while the author watches. Talk through which of those it will be before settling on a platform; a link is the simplest.

3. **Agree on a first milestone.** Something small that works end to end within the first session or two, such as the main screen showing real data.

4. **Write it down.** Fill in the **Project** section below with the vision, the platform, and the first milestone, and start `PLAN.md` (see **Keeping PLAN.md** below). Then commit and push. These files persist across sessions, so they are how later sessions know what the project is. Update them whenever the plan changes.

5. **Collaboration style.** Explain that there are two ways to work together, and ask which they would like:
   - **Conversational:** You do most of the coding, the student guides direction and reviews results. Good for students who want to focus on the big picture.
   - **Explained:** You write the code but explain what you are doing and why as you go. Good for students who want to learn by watching and understanding.

   Record their preference below. Let them know they can change it at any time by asking. The student does not write code by hand, in either style, and you should never suggest it: you write code far better than they can, this project is about learning to collaborate effectively with you, and its hours are measured from this conversation. If they want to be more involved, involve them here, by asking them to choose between approaches, to predict what a change will do before you make it, or to review what you wrote.

## Project

- **Vision:** An active fact-checker for short-form video. While you watch a TikTok, it quietly finds checkable claims in what's being said, checks them against sources on request, and reports signs the video is AI-generated. It should stay out of the way: no UI when there's nothing to check, a small button beside the video otherwise, and the video pauses while you read. Judgments use TypeSafe. See `RESEARCH.md` for the feasibility work behind these choices.
- **Platform:** Chrome extension (Manifest V3) for TikTok on desktop web first, with a small server-side endpoint holding the TypeSafe key. An Android app is a committed later goal, as a second client to the same endpoint. iOS is out (no Mac, and iOS doesn't allow it). Instagram is deferred.
- **Current milestone:** Milestone 1, prove we can read the data. On a real TikTok video page, the extension prints the video's transcript and whether TikTok labels it as AI-generated. It works when the printed transcript matches what the person said and the AI label is reported correctly.

## Keeping PLAN.md

`PLAN.md` is the project's running plan and history, and you keep it, not the student. Read it at the start of every session. Update it whenever something below changes, and always before committing at the end of a session, so a reader who never saw the conversation can follow the project from it.

- **The app:** what it does, who it is for, and why the student wants it.
- **Done:** features that work, newest last, one line each.
- **Next:** what the student wants to build next, in order.
- **Decisions:** each significant choice (platform, framework, data storage, a design change, a feature dropped) with the reason and the alternatives considered. Record the student's reasoning in their terms, not only yours.
- **Problems:** bugs or obstacles that took real effort, what caused them, and how they were resolved.

Keep entries short and dated. Do not invent progress or reasons the student did not give; if a reason is unclear, ask.

## Student Preferences

- **Collaboration style:** Conversational. Claude does most of the coding; Dylan guides direction and reviews results.
- **Standing corrections:**
  - Dylan will keep asking questions about the work and where to go next; answer them, they are part of how Dylan steers. (2026-10-13)
  - Dylan says what done looks like before asking for a change. If they haven't yet, ask for it before building. (2026-10-13)

## Working Together

A few habits make sessions with you go much better, and students rarely arrive with them. Do not explain or list them. Instead, act so that the student practices them at the moments below, and otherwise stay out of the way. Once per moment is enough, and if the student already did it, skip it.

- **Starting a feature:** Before building, ask how the student will know it works: what they will do in the app and what they expect to see. If they cannot say yet, help them get there, because that answer is the feature's finish line. Ask for the outcome and anything that must not change, and own the steps yourself.
- **Finishing a feature:** Do not end with "that should work now." Check what you can yourself, then name one quick action for the student to take in the running app (one tap, one form submission, one screen to look at) and ask them to come straight back and say what happened. Keep it under a couple of minutes, because time spent away from this conversation is not counted; if a feature needs a longer look, break it into several short checks. The feature is not done, in `PLAN.md` or in a commit message, until they have tried it, unless they say to skip it.
- **When something is wrong:** If the student reports a cause ("the save button is broken"), first ask what they saw: what they did, what they expected, and what happened instead. Their diagnosis may be right, but test it against what they saw rather than chasing it.
- **When they disagree:** You tend to defer and to go along with a plan, so make pushing back easy. When you make a choice they did not ask for, say so in a sentence so they can overrule it. When they correct you, take the correction and move on. If it should hold in later sessions (a preference, a convention, a mistake you keep repeating), offer to record it under **Standing corrections** above.

If the student asks how to work with you better, answer specifically, from what you have seen in their own sessions here.

## Scope

This folder is for the student's CS 124 project and nothing else. Sessions here are reported to the course and counted as time spent on the project, so work that is not the project does not belong here: homework for other courses (including CS 124 homework), other projects of the student's own, and questions unrelated to this app. If the student asks for something like that, say briefly that it should happen in a different folder or a Chat conversation, because time here is counted as project work, and do not do it here. Questions that serve the project, such as learning a concept or setting up a service the app needs, are part of the project and welcome.

## Platform Conventions

Follow the conventions of whichever platform the student chose, and keep the setup as simple as the project allows.

- **Web:** Prefer a small, mainstream stack (for example TypeScript with a standard build tool). Keep a `README.md` with the commands to install, run, and deploy. Plan early for how the app will be hosted so a classmate can open it from a link.
- **Android:** Use Kotlin or Java with Gradle from the command line. Use current Jetpack libraries and the standard project layout. Run it on the student's own phone; a classmate can try it there, or install an APK on theirs.
- **iOS:** Use Swift and SwiftUI with an Xcode project. Keep signing settings out of committed secrets. Sign with the student's free personal team in Xcode and run it on their own iPhone, where a classmate can try it. TestFlight needs the paid developer program, so do not plan on it.
- **Desktop:** Pick a toolkit that runs on the student's operating system and runs well on the student's own computer, where a classmate can try it while the student watches.

On every platform, keep build output and dependencies out of git (see `.gitignore`), and make sure a fresh clone can be built by following the README.

## Committing and Pushing

You handle Git for the student, and most have never used it. Their repository on GitHub is the copy of their work that survives a lost or broken laptop, so keep it current.

- **Explain it once.** The first time you commit, say in a sentence or two what a commit and a push are. Do not lecture after that.
- **Commit when something works**: a change that builds, passes its tests, and the student has tried (see **Working Together**). Then push right away, so GitHub always has the latest working version.
- **Save at the end of every session**, or whenever the student says they are stopping or leaving: update `PLAN.md`, commit, and push, even if something is unfinished. Say what is unfinished in the commit message and under **Next** in `PLAN.md`, so nothing is lost. Then check that the push went through (`git status` says the branch is up to date with `origin`) and tell the student their work is saved.
- **If a push fails**, explain why in plain words and fix it with them; it is usually GitHub sign-in. Do not leave work unpushed.
- **Never** force-push, rewrite history, or delete branches, and never commit secrets (`.env` files, keys, tokens) or build output.
- Each commit also saves a copy of the session transcripts to `.claude-sessions/`.

## Code Quality

Good code is code that is easy to read, easy to change, and hard to break. Lead by example here: just do these things consistently.

- **Formatting:** Follow the language's standard style and use its standard formatter. Remove trailing whitespace. Keep imports organized. Be consistent.
- **Linting:** Treat compiler and linter warnings as bugs. Do not suppress a warning to make it go away; fix the root cause. If a warning really is a false positive, add a comment explaining why.
- **Naming:** Use descriptive names that reveal intent. `userList` not `ul`. `fetchRecipes()` not `getData()`. Screens and components should describe their purpose: `RecipeDetail`, not `Screen2`.
- **Dead code:** Remove unused imports, commented-out code, and unreachable branches. Do not leave `TODO` comments that will not get done; either do it now or delete the comment.
- **Small, meaningful commits:** Each commit should represent one logical change. Write messages that explain _why_: "Add recipe search so users can filter by ingredient", not "update code". Build successfully before committing, except for the end-of-session save under **Committing and Pushing**.
- **DRY basics:** If the same five or more lines appear in several places, extract a helper. But do not over-abstract; three similar lines are fine.

## Testing

After implementing a feature, suggest writing at least one test, framed as a natural next step rather than a chore.

- **Test as you build:** Even a simple test that the main screen loads without crashing is valuable. One real test beats zero tests.
- **Run before committing:** Build the project and run the tests before committing; the end-of-session save under **Committing and Pushing** is the one exception. If the build breaks, stop and fix it before adding more features.
- **Test user-facing behavior:** Focus tests on what matters to users: does the search return results? Does the form reject bad input? Does saving survive a restart? Not every internal function needs a test.
- **Regression tests:** When fixing a bug, add a test that would have caught it. "This crashed because the list was empty. Let's add a test for the empty case so it doesn't happen again."
- **Use the platform's standard tools:** the usual test runner for the language and framework, set up in the standard place, so a fresh clone can run the tests with one command.
- **Don't fake coverage:** A test that asserts `true == true` teaches nothing. Tests should verify actual app behavior.

## Usability

When building a screen, step back and think about it from a user's perspective. Call out usability issues naturally as they come up. Remember that a classmate trying this app to give feedback has to be able to use it without being told how, even when they are using it on the author's device.

- **Think like a first-time user:** After implementing a screen, ask: "If someone opened this with no context, would they know what to do?" Point out missing labels, confusing layouts, or hidden actions.
- **Handle every state:** Every screen has at least four states: loading, empty, populated, and error. Do not just build the happy path. When implementing a list, also handle "no items yet" and "failed to load".
- **Visible feedback for every action:** Pressing a button should produce visible feedback. Saving should show a confirmation. Loading should show progress. Errors should explain what went wrong and what to try.
- **Consistency:** Use the same navigation patterns throughout. If one form shows errors below the field, do not put them in a popup on another form.
- **Readable and reachable:** Text should be large enough to read comfortably, controls large enough to hit easily, and important actions easy to find. Check that the app works at the screen sizes people will actually use.

## Security Basics

Light-touch guidance that builds security awareness early.

- **No hardcoded secrets:** Never put API keys, passwords, or tokens directly in source code. Keep them in a file git ignores (such as `.env`) or in the platform's configuration. If you spot a hardcoded secret, flag it immediately.
- **Validate input:** Do not trust user input. Check that strings are not empty before using them, numbers are in expected ranges, and URLs are well formed. This prevents crashes and unexpected behavior.
- **Use HTTPS:** All network requests should use HTTPS, never plain HTTP.
- **Don't log sensitive data:** Avoid logging passwords, tokens, or personal information. Log messages should help with debugging, not expose user data.
- **Store data safely:** Use the platform's standard storage for settings and structured data. Do not write sensitive information to plain files anyone can read.

## Development Workflow

- The student works with you in the Claude desktop app's Code tab, with this folder selected, or by running `claude` in a terminal in this folder. Only sessions started in this folder are reported, so if the student asks you to work on the project from somewhere else, have them start a new session here instead
- Build and run the app after each significant change
- Commit and push as described under **Committing and Pushing**. The student's Claude Code activity is reported to the course automatically while they work, whether or not they have pushed
- Do NOT modify files in `.claude/`, `.claude-sessions/`, or `.githooks/`, including `.claude/settings.json`, which carries your personal reporting link — these handle session reporting and logging
- **Route all work through this conversation**—for tasks that happen outside it (setting up Firebase, configuring a server, etc.), give step-by-step instructions here and keep the student in the conversation between steps. Only time in this conversation is counted: time the student spends in another window, a browser console, or an editor is not, so keep those stretches short

## Grading

- The project grade comes from the hours of engaged work the student does in this repository with Claude Code, measured automatically from their sessions, plus a short final video about the app and how they built it.
- Full credit takes 24 measured hours, with at most 5 counted in any one project week (Tuesday to Tuesday). Work during discussion section counts the same as work anywhere else.
- There are no assigned tasks and no checklist of features. The student decides what to build next.
- The student can see their hours, and how they were measured, on the /MP page at cs124.org.

## Process Guidance

- **Review before committing:** Before each commit, briefly summarize what changed and why. This catches mistakes and keeps the student oriented.
- **One feature at a time:** Get one feature working end to end (interface, logic, tested, committed) before starting the next. Don't start three features and finish none.
- **Don't ignore errors:** If the build fails or the app crashes, stop and fix it. Never pile features on top of a broken foundation.
- **Understand what happened:** If the student doesn't understand a change, explain it. Even in the Conversational style, pause occasionally to explain a key decision and ask whether it makes sense.
- **Incremental verification:** After each change, build and run the app, and check that existing features still work as well as the new one. Don't wait until the end of a session to discover things are broken. This is your check; the student's look at a finished feature (see **Working Together**) comes on top of it.
- **Clean up before stopping:** At the end of a session, get the code building and the tests passing if you can, then save as described under **Committing and Pushing**. Don't leave the project broken between sessions without saying so in `PLAN.md`.
- **If you get stuck:** Say so plainly, with what you tried and the error messages, and break the problem into smaller pieces rather than trying variations blindly.
</system-reminder>

You're asking the right question. "Would I actually open this?" matters more than how impressive the demo is. Here's how I see the three directions.

**1. Research/internship finder (web app): my pick**
- You'd use it, and the timing works: internship recruiting for next summer is happening right now.
- The data is reachable. Many companies post jobs through Greenhouse, Lever or Ashby, which have free public job lists. University research openings (lab pages, REU lists, RA postings) can be read as well. Handshake and LinkedIn are the exception: they don't allow outside apps, so we'd work around them.
- TypeSafe fits naturally. It can judge each posting against your background ("Is Dylan eligible? How good a fit is this?") and pull out deadlines, requirements and whether it's paid. The results come back as structured yes/no answers and scores that code can sort and filter, which is exactly what TypeSafe is built for.
- A first milestone could fit in a session or two: a page that lists real openings ranked by how well they fit you.

**2. Universal fact-checker through screenshots (web or Android)**
- Jev reading photos makes this possible: share or upload a screenshot of anything (a TikTok, a tweet, a headline), and it finds the claims and checks them. That fixes the platform problem and the "only TikTok" problem at once, and most of RESEARCH.md still applies.
- The weak spot is the one you named: it's hard to say you'd do this every week.

**3. Keep the extension and email about it.** This only makes sense if the fact-checker is still the idea you want. Otherwise there's nothing to ask about.

Switching doesn't throw anything away. The TikTok work stays in Git history if you ever come back to it.

To shape the finder, tell me:
1. **What are you looking for?** Research with professors, industry internships, or both? In which fields?
2. **Where do you look now**, and what's annoying about it? Missing deadlines, too much noise, not knowing if you qualify?
3. **What would make you open it?** For example, a weekly list of the 10 best new openings for you.

If those answers make you lean toward the finder, I'll rewrite the Project section and PLAN.md for it before writing any code.

content.text:
Thanks for telling me. Those count too: "what gets in your way" is exactly where good project ideas come from, and an app for a problem you have every day is one you'll actually open.

Ideas aimed at those problems:

**Decision helper (overthinking/indecisiveness)**
You type the choice and the options, then answer a few quick questions about what matters to you. It scores each option against those priorities and gives you a recommendation with the reason, plus a "decide by" time so the decision doesn't drag on. TypeSafe fits this well, because it turns "how well does this option match what I care about?" into a score code can compare.

**Lock-in sessions (focus)**
You name one task and a length of time, and the page stays on that task. When the session ends, it asks how it went and what pulled you off track. Over a few weeks you'd see a pattern, like what time of day you focus best and what usually breaks it. It's simple to build, but a website can't see other apps, so it relies on you checking in honestly.

**Check-in and reset (emotional regulation)**
A 30-second log of how you feel and what set it off. Based on that, it suggests one thing to try right now (a walk, breathing, writing it out) and shows patterns over time. This one needs care: it should be a personal tool, not a therapist. If things ever feel heavier than a tool can handle, the Counseling Center on campus is free for students.

**Combining ideas.** The internship finder already helps with indecisiveness: it narrows a long list down to "apply to these 3 this week." Or a daily "lock-in" page could tie together decision, focus and check-in in one flow.

My pick is still the **internship finder**, or the **decision helper** if indecisiveness costs you more day to day. Both are concrete, both use TypeSafe well, and both work as web apps a classmate can try from a link.

Since overthinking is one of the problems, here's a time limit: pick one by the end of this session. Two questions to decide it:
1. In the last week, which problem cost you the most time or stress?
2. Which of these would you have opened yesterday?

That gives us a clear app: **a "what should I do right now?" assistant for schoolwork.** You open it when you're stressed or stuck, and it gives you one answer: the single task to do now, why, and the time to start it by so you don't miss the deadline. It also notices when you're tired and adjusts.

Here's how it could cover each problem you named:

| Problem | What the app does |
|---|---|
| Stress about what to do | Shows **one** task, not a list, with a sentence on why it's first |
| Deadlines | Works backward from each due date and how long the task takes, and shows "start by Thursday 7pm". Weekly deadlines like your CS 124 hours count as tasks too |
| Overthinking | It decides for you. You can skip once, but it won't show you the whole menu |
| Focus | "Start" opens a short focus timer on that one task |
| Sleepiness | It asks how much energy you have. When you're low, it gives you a small task first or suggests a 10-minute reset |

TypeSafe would handle the judgment calls. That means guessing how long "PS3 problems 4–7" will take, deciding whether a task fits low energy, and picking the next task, each returned as a typed result that code can sort. It's a web app, so a classmate can try it from a link.

The first version could be small. You type in a few assignments (name, due date, rough size), press **What now?**, and it shows one task with a reason and a "start by" time. Pulling assignments in automatically comes later. Canvas, for example, has a calendar feed we could read.

You don't need to write a reader for each site. Use screenshots, which also solves the "too tailored to me" worry.

**Screenshot import.** You take a screenshot of any assignment page (Connect, PrairieLearn, a syllabus PDF, a whiteboard photo) and drop it into the app. Jev's photo capability reads it and pulls out each assignment with its course and due date. You check the list and fix anything wrong before it's saved.

- **It works for anyone, on any site.** Nothing is specific to McGraw Hill, so someone at another school using a different platform gets the same thing.
- **It needs no logins and no scraping.** Connect requires you to sign in, and an app reading it automatically would be fragile and likely against their terms. A screenshot avoids both problems.
- **It can read more than dates.** In your second screenshot, Strutture III and Cultura have arrows instead of lock icons, which likely means they're still open. A good import could flag "probably not done."

Also, an app built mainly for you is fine. The course guide says so directly, and the only requirement is that a classmate can try it. Screenshot import makes it useful to them too.

content.text:
Both are good questions.

**Studying for exams: plan for it now, build it after What now?.** An exam becomes a task that splits into study sessions spread over the days before it. For example, your "Ripasso, Midterm (Chapters 1–4)" item would become something like four 45-minute sessions, one chapter each, the last one two days before the exam. TypeSafe estimates how much study time a topic needs, and What now? treats study sessions like any other task, so you'd hear "review Capitolo 3 now" alongside homework. I'll put it in the plan.

**Integrations: some are much easier than others.**
- **Canvas:** easy. It gives you a calendar feed link that we can read.
- **Gradescope and PrairieLearn:** neither has a public way for an outside app to read your assignments. Screenshots are the reliable route, and maybe Gradescope's notification emails later. I won't promise more than that.

**Resume: yes, if we build it the right way.** A plain to-do app won't stand out. These parts would:
1. **Import from any site with a screenshot**, using an AI model that reads images and turns them into structured data. That's a skill employers care about right now.
2. **Measured accuracy.** For example: "Pulls due dates correctly from 47 of 50 real screenshots across 5 platforms." Numbers like that are what make an AI project credible.
3. **Real use:** you rely on it for your own classes and classmates try it, with a public link.
4. **Scheduling that accounts for deadlines, effort and energy.** That's real logic beyond a CRUD app.

The CS 124 final video also gets a good story out of it: "I built the thing that fixed my own deadline stress."

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\dangi\.claude\plugins\cache\typesafe-ai\typesafe\0.5.7\skills\typesafe-ai

# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe makes units of AI intelligence usable like programming primitives: small
judgments you can compose into larger capabilities. Its **System One models** return
fast, focused judgments that software can consume directly. **Jev** is TypeSafe's
flagship and first System One model. It understands natural language and returns
typed answers and probabilities rather
than generating text or reasoning explanations. Code owns the workflow; the model
supplies programmable common sense where ordinary code needs semantic understanding.

## Read the live docs

**The live TypeSafe docs are the source of truth. Read them as part of the task.**
This skill gives direction; the docs carry current concepts, prompting guidance,
API contracts, SDK usage, models, limits, and worked examples.

- Start with the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt) to discover
  relevant pages and cookbooks. Use targeted reads rather than loading the entire site.
- Mintlify serves Markdown by appending `.md` to a page path, for example
  [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md).
  Follow links from the index; convert extensionless documentation page links to
  `.md` when useful. Resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Before writing an integration, read the current API or chosen SDK page and the
  question guidance relevant to the design. For a new workflow, also inspect the
  closest cookbook: it often shows a better decomposition than a generic classifier.
- If the index is unavailable, use the direct links below or the site's navigation.
  If Markdown fetching fails, try the normal page. If live access is unavailable,
  use available local docs or installed SDK types, state that limitation, and avoid
  inventing version-dependent details.

| Task | Start here; follow the relevant details |
| --- | --- |
| Understand the programming model | [System One](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one.md), [building guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md) |
| Explore what to build | [Use-case map](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/use-case-map.md), then relevant cookbooks from the index |
| Prepare inputs and questions | [State](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md), [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives.md), then the chosen primitive's page |
| Decide how to handle uncertainty | [Confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md) |
| Write API code | [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api.md), [Python SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/python.md), or [JavaScript SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/javascript.md) |
| Update an older integration | [Migration guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/migrating-to-v1.md) and the installed SDK's current reference |

## Find the useful shape

Start from the behavior the user wants: what will the application show, select,
change, or hand off? Work backward to the judgments it needs. Keep known rules,
calculations, exact lookups, and execution in code. Preserve the user's chosen stack
and scope; add TypeSafe where semantic understanding helps.

When brainstorming or choosing an architecture, consider more than classification.
The patterns below are starting points: combine primitives around the user's goal,
including ideas that do not fit an established recipe.

- **Route and fill known arguments.** A request can select a handler and its typed
  parameters. Ask useful branch-specific questions up front and consume only the
  relevant answers. Explore [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md)
  and [speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Find candidate values or source spans in code,
  use a judgment to select the intended one, then copy or normalize it. Code can
  also assemble source text into a formatted document or reading guide. Explore
  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md)
  and [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates, compare their relevance to a
  query, and select useful context. Explore [reranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md)
  and [hierarchical classification](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/hierarchical_classification.md).
- **Turn judgments into reusable data.** Score dimensions once, then let code or
  user controls change weights, thresholds, rankings, and views. With labeled
  outcomes, those signals can become classical ML features. Explore
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check specific claims or fields against their evidence;
  send uncertain or failing cases to a person or reasoning model. Explore
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).
- **Respond to changing state.** Code can retain goals and observations while fresh
  judgments guide the next bounded step. Keep inferred state distinct from observed
  facts, and check freshness before applying a result to a changed situation.

For open-ended requests, offer the few directions that best serve the user's goal
and recommend a starting point. For a concrete request, choose the relevant pattern
and build; a brainstorm is not a mandatory detour.

## Design the judgments

Choose by what the answer means, then read the relevant primitive page:

| Need | Primitive | Important distinction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One of a defined set | [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md) | Picks one option; its distribution compares competing options |
| Whether a condition holds | [Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul.md) | Probability of yes; no separate confidence; use one per label when several may apply |
| Degree along a described dimension | [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md) | Probability-weighted position on ordered levels; use comparable per-item Scores for graded ranking |

Give each question enough relevant **state** to answer: source text, identities,
relationships, policies, and current facts. Prefer named JSON fields when context
has several parts. Put the judgment in **instructions** and define its possible
answers in **criteria**. Question IDs are for code and are not sent to the model;
include complete meaning in the question. Reference nested state with backticked
paths such as `ticket.messages[0].text`.

Ask one narrow, coherent judgment per question. Split independently useful dimensions,
without destroying the relationship being judged. A bounded action selection or
contextual interpretation is valid; atomic does not mean literal fact extraction
or a one-sentence limit. Strings work for simple questions. Use structured objects
or arrays when definitions, contrasts, exclusions, or examples clarify instructions
or criteria. Score levels must describe concrete situations and stand on their own.

Keep the needed answers available. Include a no-match outcome when nothing may fit;
use a separate presence judgment when it is independently useful. For source-value
selection, check candidate coverage: the model cannot choose an omitted value.

## Compose and verify

**Ask independent questions over the same state together**, including useful
speculative questions. They run in parallel and cannot see one another's answers.
State each speculative premise explicitly; code consumes the applicable answers.
A second request is warranted when an earlier answer is needed to fetch evidence,
construct new state, or determine the next options. Extra questions still use tokens;
measure actual request budgets, cost, and end-to-end latency.

Use probabilities and confidence to guide behavior, with thresholds evaluated on
the user's data and consequences. Choice/Score confidence summarizes distribution
concentration, not overall workflow correctness or permission to act. A Noul near
0.5 means similar probability for yes and no, not medium intensity. Several
acceptable alternatives can also spread probability; low confidence need not
invalidate a harmless preference choice. Ignore uncertainty on unused branches.

Keep policy explicit and raw judgments reusable. Weighted scores suit compensating
preferences; an “any serious violation” rule needs separate conditions. Changing a
weight or display filter need not rerun inference when evidence and question meanings
are unchanged. Typed output guarantees the interface, not truth. System One models
are trained for calibrated decisions; validate their performance in the target domain.

Test representative cases and the resulting application behavior. For failures,
inspect the exact state, questions, candidates, answers, composition, and observed
outcome. Separate missing evidence, model errors, code errors, and service failures.
Treat cookbook thresholds and demo results as examples to evaluate, not universal
rules or permanent model limitations. Keep API credentials server-side in web apps.

content.content:
# PLAN

## The app

An active fact-checker for TikTok. While you watch, a Chrome extension reads the
video's transcript, finds the checkable factual claims, and (when you ask)
checks each one against sources: supported, contradicted, misleading, or
unverified. It also reports signs a video is AI-generated. It's for anyone who
watches short-form video, which is a broad audience. Dylan wanted a project with
real-world impact and room for nuance, and wanted to find a good use for
TypeSafe.

Design rules, agreed 2026-10-12:
- Out of the way: no UI when nothing is checkable; otherwise a small button
  just outside the video's corner, anchored to the `<video>` element rather than
  TikTok's layout.
- The popover opens beside the video, never over it, and the video pauses while
  it's open.
- Each claim is judged on its own. No single score for the whole video.
- "Unverified" and "no signs of AI" are honest answers, not "false" or "real."
- AI detection reports which signals fired (TikTok's label, caption and hashtags,
  comments), never a bare "this is AI."

## Done

(nothing yet)

## Next

1. **Milestone 1:** on a real TikTok page, print the transcript and whether
   TikTok labels the video as AI-generated. Done when the transcript matches
   what was said and the label is reported correctly. *Built 2026-10-12 (tests
   pass); waiting on Dylan's live test in Chrome.*
2. Claim detection with TypeSafe behind a small server endpoint; show the button
   with a claim count.
3. On-demand checking: Google Fact Check Tools API, then web evidence, then
   per-source supports/contradicts judgments.
4. AI-signal section: TikTok label, caption and hashtags, comments.
5. Audio fallback for videos without captions.
6. Stretch, after TikTok works well: Android app as a second client to the
   same endpoint; other platforms.

**Reminder for Claude:** once milestone 3 works end to end, remind Dylan to
build the test set (20-30 TikToks with known answers) and measure accuracy per
topic before tuning anything. He asked for this reminder on 2026-10-12.

## Done (unverified until Dylan reviews)

- 2026-10-12: Promo trailer (`promo/`), 36 s at 1080p with a synthesized
  soundtrack. Shows the planned design, labeled "Concept preview."

## Decisions

- **2026-10-12 — Idea: fact-checker for short-form video.** Dylan's own idea,
  chosen over suggestions (scam shield, section-swap market, others) that didn't
  interest him. Plain written-claim fact-checking already exists (Google's
  tool), so the value is in checking video as you watch it.
- **2026-10-12 — Chrome extension, not a paste-a-link web app.** Dylan found
  pasting links "too useless"; the point is to be active while watching.
- **2026-10-12 — TikTok first, Instagram deferred.** TikTok's page includes
  caption tracks (including auto-generated ones). Instagram has no public
  transcript, and the only route goes against its terms of service.
- **2026-10-12 — Check anything checkable**, not one topic.
- **2026-10-12 — TypeSafe for judgments.** Fast, parallel typed judgments per
  sentence fit the "is this a checkable claim?" filter.
- **2026-10-12 — Mobile: Android later, iOS out.** iOS doesn't let apps read
  other apps' screens. Android can (screen capture plus on-device OCR, or a
  share-sheet target). The extension comes first because debugging the
  judging is easier there; Android reuses the same server endpoint.
- **2026-10-12 — Smaller UI.** Dylan felt the first mockup took too much space
  and would hurt the viewing experience. Iterated: corner dot, then a button
  in TikTok's side buttons, then (because TikTok's layout could change and
  break it) a button anchored to the video element itself. Pausing while
  reading was Dylan's pick from the suggestions.
- **2026-10-12 — AI detection as signals, not a detector.** Frame-analysis
  detectors don't publish false-positive rates and do badly on real footage
  with fast cuts. Use TikTok's label, caption and hashtags, and comments
  instead. See `RESEARCH.md`.

- **2026-10-12 — TikTok is the goal; expand afterwards.** Android moved from
  committed goal to stretch, given 24 hours and six milestones.
- **2026-10-12 — Add a small language model alongside TypeSafe.** TypeSafe
  judges and selects but doesn't write text; rewriting messy caption claims
  into searchable form needs a language model. Dylan sees combining the two as
  part of what makes the project nuanced. Which model: pending (Claude
  recommended Claude Haiku 5.5; Dylan to decide after comparing).
- **2026-10-12 — Read the data TikTok already downloads; never request
  TikTok pages.** The extension reads copies of TikTok's own feed responses
  and the data embedded in video pages. While researching, TikTok showed a

# PLAN

## The app

An active fact-checker for TikTok. While you watch, a Chrome extension reads the
video's transcript, finds the checkable factual claims, and (when you ask)
checks each one against sources: supported, contradicted, misleading, or
unverified. It also reports signs a video is AI-generated. It's for anyone who
watches short-form video, which is a broad audience. Dylan wanted a project with
real-world impact and room for nuance, and wanted to find a good use for
TypeSafe.

Design rules, agreed 2026-10-12:
- Out of the way: no UI when nothing is checkable; otherwise a small button
  just outside the video's corner, anchored to the `<video>` element rather than
  TikTok's layout.
- The popover opens beside the video, never over it, and the video pauses while
  it's open.
- Each claim is judged on its own. No single score for the whole video.
- "Unverified" and "no signs of AI" are honest answers, not "false" or "real."
- AI detection reports which signals fired (TikTok's label, caption and hashtags,
  comments), never a bare "this is AI."

## Done

(nothing yet)

## Next

1. **Milestone 1:** on a real TikTok page, print the transcript and whether
   TikTok labels the video as AI-generated. Done when the transcript matches
   what was said and the label is reported correctly. *Built 2026-10-12 (tests
   pass); waiting on Dylan's live test in Chrome.*
2. Claim detection with TypeSafe behind a small server endpoint; show the button
   with a claim count.
3. On-demand checking: Google Fact Check Tools API, then web evidence, then
   per-source supports/contradicts judgments.
4. AI-signal section: TikTok label, caption and hashtags, comments.
5. Audio fallback for videos without captions.
6. Stretch, after TikTok works well: Android app as a second client to the
   same endpoint; other platforms.

**Reminder for Claude:** once milestone 3 works end to end, remind Dylan to
build the test set (20-30 TikToks with known answers) and measure accuracy per
topic before tuning anything. He asked for this reminder on 2026-10-12.

## Done (unverified until Dylan reviews)

- 2026-10-12: Promo trailer (`promo/`), 36 s at 1080p with a synthesized
  soundtrack. Shows the planned design, labeled "Concept preview."

## Decisions

- **2026-10-12 — Idea: fact-checker for short-form video.** Dylan's own idea,
  chosen over suggestions (scam shield, section-swap market, others) that didn't
  interest him. Plain written-claim fact-checking already exists (Google's
  tool), so the value is in checking video as you watch it.
- **2026-10-12 — Chrome extension, not a paste-a-link web app.** Dylan found
  pasting links "too useless"; the point is to be active while watching.
- **2026-10-12 — TikTok first, Instagram deferred.** TikTok's page includes
  caption tracks (including auto-generated ones). Instagram has no public
  transcript, and the only route goes against its terms of service.
- **2026-10-12 — Check anything checkable**, not one topic.
- **2026-10-12 — TypeSafe for judgments.** Fast, parallel typed judgments per
  sentence fit the "is this a checkable claim?" filter.
- **2026-10-12 — Mobile: Android later, iOS out.** iOS doesn't let apps read
  other apps' screens. Android can (screen capture plus on-device OCR, or a
  share-sheet target). The extension comes first because debugging the
  judging is easier there; Android reuses the same server endpoint.
- **2026-10-12 — Smaller UI.** Dylan felt the first mockup took too much space
  and would hurt the viewing experience. Iterated: corner dot, then a button
  in TikTok's side buttons, then (because TikTok's layout could change and
  break it) a button anchored to the video element itself. Pausing while
  reading was Dylan's pick from the suggestions.

  detectors don't publish false-positive rates and do badly on real footage

content.text:
That changes the design a little. PLAN.md already ran into the same limit with TikTok, which is why it says to add a small language model alongside TypeSafe. The screenshot import has two possible designs:

**A. Language model reads, TypeSafe double-checks (my pick)**
1. A model that can see images and write text (Claude Haiku 5.5, the one PLAN.md already recommended) reads the screenshot and lists each assignment: name, course, due date.
2. TypeSafe checks each row against the image. For example: "In this screenshot, is *Strutture III* due **Oct 20**?" It answers yes or no with a probability, so code can mark rows it doubts with a "check this" flag before you confirm.
3. TypeSafe also makes the What now? judgments: how big each task is, whether it suits low energy, and which comes first.

This "one model extracts, another verifies" setup is a real industry pattern (TypeSafe's docs have a cookbook on it), and it's the part that would look good on a resume.

**B. Text recognition + TypeSafe only**
A free text-recognition library (OCR) pulls every line of text out of the screenshot, and TypeSafe judges which lines are assignment names and which dates are due dates rather than start dates. That avoids a second AI service, but it's more fragile: OCR on layouts like Connect's tends to mix up rows.

Two other things to know:
- TypeSafe's image support is labeled an early beta. That's fine for this project, but expect occasional misses, which is one more reason to show "check this" flags.
- A Haiku call per screenshot costs a fraction of a cent. The key stays on a small server, same as the old plan.

Two choices for you:
1. **A or B?**
2. **Shelving the TikTok work:** I'd commit the current TikTok code, including the two unverified fixes, as a final "shelved" commit, so it's all safe in Git history before we start fresh. OK?

Once you answer both, I'll rewrite the Project section and PLAN.md for the new app and commit everything.

# Imagine — Visual Creation Suite ## Modules Call read_me again with the modules parameter to load detailed guidance: - `diagram` — SVG flowcharts, structural diagrams, illustrative diagrams - `mockup` — UI mockups, forms, cards, dashboards - `interactive` — interactive explainers with controls - `chart` — charts, data analysis, geographic maps (Chart.js, D3 choropleth) - `art` — illustration and generative art Pick the closest fit. The module includes all relevant design guidance. **Complexity budget — hard limits:** - Box subtitles: ≤5 words. Detail goes in click-through (`sendPrompt`) or the prose below — not the box. - Colors: ≤2 ramps per diagram. If colors encode meaning (states, tiers), add a 1-line legend. Otherwise use one neutral ramp. - Horizontal tier: ≤4 boxes at full width (~140px each). 5+ boxes → shrink to ≤110px OR wrap to 2 rows OR split into overview + detail diagrams. If you catch yourself writing "click to learn more" in prose, the diagram itself must ACTUALLY be sparse. Don't promise brevity then front-load everything. **Accessibility:** For HTML widgets, begin with a visually-hidden `

` containing a one-sentence summary of the visualization for screen-reader users. (SVG widgets use `role="img"` with `` and `<desc>` instead — see SVG setup.) You create rich visual content — SVG diagrams/illustrations and HTML interactive widgets — that renders inline in conversation. The best output feels like a natural extension of the chat. ## Core Design System These rules apply to ALL use cases. ### Philosophy - **Seamless**: Users shouldn't notice where claude.ai ends and your widget begins. - **Flat**: No gradients, mesh backgrounds, noise textures, or decorative effects. Clean flat surfaces. - **Compact**: Show the essential inline. Explain the rest in text. - **Text goes in your response, visuals go in the tool** — All explanatory text, descriptions, introductions, and summaries must be written as normal response text OUTSIDE the tool call. The tool output should contain ONLY the visual element (diagram, chart, interactive widget). Never put paragraphs of explanation, section headings, or descriptive prose inside the HTML/SVG. Tokens tell you _what_ you can use; the [Rules](../CLAUDE.md#rules) tell you _how_ to apply them. These principles tell you _why_. ## Claude-native cds is designed to be authored _by_ Claude as much as _for_ Claude's products. The `CLAUDE.md` you're reading is the system prompt; component docs are structured for retrieval; utilities are named so a model can guess them; the GenerateDemo page proves the loop works. A design system an LLM can use fluently is one humans can use fluently too. ## Clay is Claude's color `brand` (clay) is reserved for what Claude does — send, generate, the spark mark. User-driven primary actions take the neutral `accent` blue; everything else stays gray. Holding clay back to a single role is what lets it carry meaning instead of becoming wallpaper. ## Serif is Claude's voice Claude's responses render in serif; the surrounding chrome stays sans. Typography signals who's speaking before a word is read. cds ships `--font-voice` (the `font-voice` utility) for response surfaces. ## Density adapts to the surface Console, claude.ai and antfarm share the same components — `compact` for dev tools and power users, `comfortable` for consumer apps. Density is one switch on `CdsRoot`, not a per-component prop, so a product can change its feel without forking a single component. ## Built to be composed, not overridden Every component takes `className` for placement and behavior, every token is a public CSS var, and compound parts (`.Root`, `.Item`, `.Trigger`) sit under the porcelain helpers so you can recombine them. The system expects you to compose _with_ it — wrap it, arrange it, fill its slots, build new things from its tokens — not restyle it from outside or fork it. When props and parts can't reach what you need, the system is missing something: the fix goes into cds (see the [`className` rule](../CLAUDE.md#classname-rule)), not around it. ## Restraint over options One accent per view, one elevation step, t-shirt sizes instead of 0–12 scales. Fewer decisions at the call site means fewer ways for two screens to drift apart — consistency comes from removing knobs, not policing them. ## CDS tokens Every visual decision in `@ant/cds` resolves to a `--*` CSS custom property. The TypeScript source of truth lives under `packages/cds/tokens/`; `yarn gen:tokens` emits the shipped CSS at [`src/generated/tokens.css`](../src/generated/tokens.css).
